title: A Warm and Koji Thanksgiving: Curry Pot Pie
contentHtml:
Japanese curry meets classic pot pie in this comforting, flaky-crusted dish that transforms leftover turkey or rotisserie chicken.

I often ate Japanese curry and chicken pot pie in close temporal proximity to each other. As I mentioned in this White Bean and Mushroom Pot Pie post, chicken pot pie was a Saturday lunch staple in the downtime between my Japanese school and music school. My mom might have then made Japanese curry for dinner on those days, too.

Given I grew up eating both several times a month, it’s not a stretch to imagine it happening on the same day. But in the same meal in the same dish? Somehow, the concept of combining curry and pot pie never occurred to me until I saw a recent video from Christopher Kimball's Milk Street suggesting it.

The idea was instantly appealing, and since I was in the throes of Thanksgiving recipe testing, I had plenty of leftover turkey, curry gravy, and frozen puff pastry from my Miso Caramel Apple Tarte Tatin to work with. The results were every bit as delicious as you'd imagine taking a comfort meal and adding a crisp, flaky, buttery crust would be. (It also works beautifully with rotisserie chicken, or with no meat at all!)

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • Japanese curry has the perfect texture for pot pie filling. The curry roux blocks do double duty here, adding the warm, sweet, and savory flavors of Japanese curry while helping thicken the gravy into the desired consistency.

  • Using leftover roast turkey or chicken makes it quick and easy. It's also a great way to use up leftover roasted or boiled vegetables (though you can use fresh ones as well).

  • A buttery, flaky, store-bought puff pastry crust adds a crisp contrast to the rich, creamy curry filling.

  • Using store-bought frozen puff pastry means you can assemble the whole thing in a single skillet without having to make pie dough or dirty extra dishes. You can also divide the filling into individual ramekins for personal-sized pies.

Yield: Serves 6 to 8
Active Time: 25 minutes
Total Time: About 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes
Notes:

  • This recipe is particularly good with leftover Koji-Brined Roast Turkey with Garlic-Scallion Mayo or rotisserie chicken, but virtually any leftover roast poultry will work. For a meatless version, omit the poultry and replace it with a few extra cups of cooked vegetables. Use vegetable stock and gravy, and check the curry roux ingredients if you're cooking for vegetarians.

  • If you have leftover roasted carrots, potatoes, parsnips, sweet potatoes, squash, or other vegetables from Thanksgiving dinner, feel free to substitute them for some or all of the fresh vegetables. Since they're already cooked, you can skip the initial simmering step and add them directly to the gravy along with the turkey or chicken.

  • The amount of curry roux you need will depend on the brand you're using and how thick and flavorful your leftover gravy already is. Start with one block and add more as needed to produce a rich texture.

  • The filling should be thick and creamy, but still loose enough to flow freely off a spoon. It will thicken a little more as it bakes and cools. Add stock or water if it's too thick, or additional curry roux if it's too thin.

  • Keep the puff pastry refrigerated until you're ready to use it. It should be fully thawed but still cold when it goes into the oven for the best puff.

Ingredients

  • 2 tablespoons (30 g) unsalted butter or neutral oil

  • 1 medium onion (about 6 oz; 170 g), diced

  • 2 medium carrots (about 6 oz; 170 g), peeled and cut into ½-inch dice

  • 1 medium Yukon Gold potato (about 8 oz; 225 g), peeled and cut into ½-inch dice

  • Leftover gravy, plus enough stock or water to make 4 cups (960 ml) total liquid

  • 1 to 3 blocks Japanese curry roux, such as S&B Golden Curry or Vermont Curry, plus more as needed

  • 3 cups (about 1 lb; 450 g) shredded cooked turkey or rotisserie chicken (optional; see notes above)

  • 1 cup (about 140 g) frozen green peas

  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper

  • 1 package frozen puff pastry, thawed (you'll need enough to cover your skillet or ramekins)

  • 1 large egg, beaten with 1 tablespoon (15 ml) water

  • Coarse or flaky sea salt, for sprinkling

Method

  1. Cook the vegetables. Adjust an oven rack to the middle position and preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Melt the butter or heat the oil in a deep, 12-inch ovenproof skillet over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots, and potatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are starting to soften, about 5 minutes. If the vegetables threaten to brown, turn down the heat.

  2. Add the gravy. Add the gravy and stock or water, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook until the carrots and potatoes are just tender, about 10 to 12 minutes. (If using leftover cooked vegetables, simply soften any raw onions in the butter, add the gravy and stock or water, bring to a simmer, and proceed to the next step, adding the cooked vegetables along with the turkey or chicken.)

  3. Make the curry filling. Crumble or finely chop one block of Japanese curry roux and stir it into the gravy until completely dissolved. Add the shredded turkey or chicken, the frozen peas, and any leftover cooked vegetables you're using. Stir to combine.

  4. Simmer and adjust. Simmer gently for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until everything is heated through and the gravy has thickened. Add more curry roux, half a block at a time, stirring to dissolve it and making sure the sauce stays at a simmer, until the curry is thick enough to look glossy and creamy but still flows freely off a spoon. Season to taste with salt and pepper and remove from the heat.

  5. Top with the pastry. Let the filling cool at room temperature for 5 to 10 minutes while you prepare the pastry. Unfold or unroll the thawed puff pastry onto a lightly floured work surface and, if necessary, roll it out until it's large enough to cover the skillet with a little overhang. Drape the pastry over the filling, pressing it gently against the rim of the skillet and trimming away any excess (or leaving it in place, if you prefer).

  6. Prepare to bake. Brush the surface with the beaten egg, sprinkle lightly with coarse salt, and cut two or three small slits in the center to allow steam to escape.

  7. Bake the pot pie. Place the skillet on a rimmed baking sheet to catch any drips and transfer to the oven. Bake until the pastry is deeply golden brown and puffed and the filling is bubbling around the edges and through the slits, 25 to 35 minutes. If the pastry is browning too quickly before the filling is bubbling, loosely tent it with foil.

  8. Rest and serve. Remove the pot pie from the oven and let it rest for 5 to 10 minutes before serving. The filling will thicken slightly as it cools.

Recipe Variation: Individual Curry Pot Pies

Prepare the filling as directed, then divide it among ovenproof ramekins, leaving about ½ inch of space at the top. Cut the puff pastry into circles slightly larger than the openings of the ramekins, drape them over the filling, and gently press the edges against the rims. Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with coarse salt, and cut a small slit in the center of each.

Arrange the ramekins on a rimmed baking sheet and bake at 425°F (220°C) until the pastry is puffed and golden brown and the filling is bubbling, 20 to 30 minutes, depending on the size of your ramekins.
